MARKET OVERVIEW
🌎 The week the sector stopped selling and started buying.

Track every space stock live at Orbit Alpha

After three weeks of unrelenting correction, the IPO rotation, the Fed repricing, the margin-call cascade, the sector did something it hadn't done since the sell-off began: it stopped falling and started making moves. Not defensive ones. Transformative ones.

Rocket Lab announced an $8 billion acquisition of Iridium Communications on 29 June, the largest pure-play space M&A deal on record, pivoting from a launch-and-components business into a vertically integrated space utility with a global satellite network, L-band spectrum, and recurring subscription revenue. ASTS surged 21% on Monday after Japan confirmed approximately ¥150 billion (~$926 million) in government subsidies for a Rakuten-led satellite network built on AST SpaceMobile's direct-to-device platform. SpaceX stabilised after its worst month as a public company and climbed back to $162 ahead of Monday's Nasdaq-100 inclusion, with Wedbush initiating coverage at Outperform. NASA awarded roughly $590 million in lunar delivery contracts to three providers in a single day. And Blue Origin laid out its path back to flight after the May pad explosion.

The tone shift was unmistakable. Where June's story was "everything is falling regardless of fundamentals," this week the market began differentiating again, rewarding catalysts, punishing nothing new. The correction may not be over, but the posture has changed: the companies with capital and conviction are deploying it, and the tape is starting to listen.

ROCKET LAB (RKLB)

This is the biggest strategic bet Peter Beck has ever made, and the market loved it. On 29 June, Rocket Lab announced a definitive agreement to acquire Iridium Communications for $54 per share in a cash-and-stock transaction, $27.00 in cash and the balance in Rocket Lab shares calculated via an exchange ratio subject to a collar banded from $67.50 to $112.50, implying an enterprise value of approximately $8 billion. The $54 offer represents a 24% premium over Iridium's 26 June closing price. The deal, expected to close mid-2027 pending Iridium shareholder approval and regulatory clearance, was unanimously approved by both boards. It merges Rocket Lab's launch services and satellite manufacturing with Iridium's global constellation of 66 active satellites and 14 on-orbit spares, its L-band spectrum, positioning/navigation/timing capabilities, and a 500-plus partner ecosystem, including the Aireon aviation-tracking business Iridium acquired in May for $367 million. The strategic logic is full vertical integration: design, build, launch, operate. The stock surged roughly 16% on Monday and continued climbing through the week, closing near $100, up roughly 25% on the week. BofA raised its price target to $115, Craig-Hallum to $120, and Roth to $130, all maintaining Buy ratings. Separately, the "Grain Goddess Provides" Electron launch for Japanese SAR operator iQPS was scrubbed on 30 June due to conditions at the pad; backup windows are available in the coming days. It would be Rocket Lab's 13th launch of 2026 and 92nd overall.

SPACEX (SPCX)

After three weeks of bleeding from its $225.64 high to a post-IPO low of $147.11, SpaceX found a floor and began to rebuild. The stock consolidated in a $149–$163 range for most of the week, then broke higher to close at $162 on Thursday 3 July, up roughly 6% on the week and its first positive week since the IPO. The near-term catalyst is Monday 7 July, when SPCX officially joins the Nasdaq-100, triggering mandatory index-fund purchases into a stock with only approximately 5% free float. Wedbush initiated coverage at Outperform on 30 June, calling SpaceX "a major hyperscaler" and anchoring the bull case on Starlink's subscription ramp and the AI division's compute agreements, including a reported $920 million-per-month deal with Google that annualises to roughly $11 billion. The August 6 earnings report, SpaceX's first as a public company, is the next fundamental test, and it doubles as the trigger for the earliest lockup release.

AST SPACEMOBILE (ASTS)

This was the week AST's Japan thesis went from rumour to funded programme. On Monday 29 June, reports confirmed that Japan will provide approximately ¥150 billion (~$926 million) in government subsidies for a low-Earth-orbit satellite communications network built around a Rakuten Mobile–AST SpaceMobile joint venture. Rakuten CEO Hiroshi Mikitani said the JV will be established this year with equal ownership and Rakuten-led management. The programme is positioned as a domestically controlled alternative to the KDDI–SpaceX Starlink consortium already operating in Japan, developed as an economic security priority to reduce dependence on foreign satellite networks. The stock surged 21% on Monday to $86.77, its best single session in nearly two years. Japan's communications ministry has separately recommended clearing the 700 MHz band for satellite-to-phone services, with rule revisions expected in September, giving Rakuten a regulatory path to direct-to-cell. Limited service is targeted for late 2026, with nationwide coverage by fiscal 2027. BlueBirds 11, 12 and 13 remain on track for a first-half-August launch from Cape Canaveral.

INTUITIVE MACHINES (LUNR)

On 30 June, NASA awarded Intuitive Machines its sixth CLPS task order, a firm-fixed-price contract valued at up to $148.3 million to deliver a production-line-qualified Nova-C lander to the Moon no later than 2028. The financial structure includes a $68.6 million base for mission execution using a lander with proven lunar flight heritage and a $79.7 million performance incentive tied to product-line qualification, effectively paying Intuitive Machines to prove it can manufacture landers at scale. CEO Steve Altemus framed it as a shift "from custom aerospace engineering to commercial mass production of lunar infrastructure." The award was part of a broader NASA CLPS round that also included Firefly ($144.2 million) and Astrobotic ($297.9 million for two deliveries), totalling roughly $590 million across three providers in a single day, the clearest signal yet that NASA is accelerating its commercial lunar logistics pipeline ahead of Artemis.

FIREFLY AEROSPACE (FLY)

Firefly's share of the 30 June NASA CLPS round was a $144.2 million contract for an accelerated Blue Ghost lunar mission, its sixth contracted lunar delivery. The same day, Firefly and SSC Space announced the completion of critical infrastructure milestones at Launch Complex 3C at Esrange Space Center in Sweden, advancing pad construction for Firefly's Alpha rocket and European orbital launch capability.

REDWIRE (RDW)

On 30 June, Redwire announced a contract to deliver its Penguin Mk2.5 VTOL uncrewed aerial system to the Taiwan Coast Guard via Taiwan Color Optics, a subsidiary of SemiLux International, a defence export win that extends the company's drone business into the Indo-Pacific. Beyond that, the stock continued to stabilise after its brutal June unwind, trading near $10–$11 with no further analyst downgrades.

BLUE ORIGIN (Private)

Blue Origin provided its first detailed recovery update on 30 June since the 28 May New Glenn pad explosion. CEO Dave Limp confirmed the company will not rebuild the destroyed launch complex to its original design but is instead pivoting to a horizontal/vertical hybrid configuration, a concept already in development for the larger 9×4 New Glenn variant, using a crane for vertical breakover at the pad rather than a traditional transporter-erector. Debris has been fully cleared and reconstruction is underway. The root cause remains under investigation, with early analysis pointing to the aft section of the first stage. Blue Origin is targeting a return to flight by year-end, a timeline widely considered aggressive given that comparable pad events have historically required a year or more to resolve. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman called Blue Origin's response "almost beyond impressive" and confirmed the agency is sticking with New Glenn as the Blue Moon lander launch vehicle, with flexibility through mid-2027 before Artemis 3 timelines are affected. For this basket, the relevance is supply: New Glenn's downtime removes a heavy-lift alternative to Falcon 9 from the manifest at a moment when launch demand is accelerating.

Takeaway: Three weeks ago this space related stocks were in freefall. This week it produced the largest space-sector M&A deal ever announced (RKLB–Iridium, $8 billion), the largest government subsidy commitment for direct-to-device infrastructure outside the US (Japan–Rakuten–ASTS, ~$926 million), nearly $600 million in NASA lunar contracts in a single day (LUNR, FLY, Astrobotic), the first analyst initiation on SpaceX as a public company (Wedbush Outperform), and a return-to-flight plan from Blue Origin. The correction isn't necessarily over, the SPCX lockup calendar, the August 6 earnings cycle, and the macro overhang are all still live. But the posture has changed. The companies that spent June absorbing a sell-off are now deploying capital, signing deals, and reshaping their competitive positions while their share prices sit 30–50% below May highs. Whether that turns out to be well-timed conviction or premature confidence is the question the second half of the year will answer. The first signal arrives Monday, when the index funds start buying SPCX.

SENTIMENT SIGNAL
🎯 THE $8 BILLION BET: WHAT ROCKET LAB IS REALLY BUYING - AND WHAT IT MEANS FOR EVERY NAME IN THE BASKET

On Sunday 29 June, Rocket Lab announced it would acquire Iridium Communications for $54 per share in a cash-and-stock transaction, an enterprise value of approximately $8 billion. The stock surged roughly 16% on Monday, every covering analyst raised their price target, and the headline across every financial outlet was some variation of "Rocket Lab versus SpaceX." That framing sells clicks. It is also wrong, and understanding why it is wrong is the most valuable thing an equity investor in this sector can take from the deal. This deep dive unpacks what Rocket Lab actually bought, why the price was rational, what it changes about the financial profile of the combined company, and what the broader consolidation wave tells you about where the rest of the basket is headed.

THE CONSOLIDATION WAVE: WHY THIS DEAL HAPPENED NOW

The Iridium acquisition did not happen in isolation. It is the fourth major space-sector consolidation event in less than twelve months, and the pattern tells a story that matters more than any single deal. SpaceX acquired EchoStar's AWS-4 and H-block spectrum, both L-band and S-band, for approximately $17 billion in late 2025, giving Starlink direct-to-cell spectrum across low and mid frequencies. SES completed its purchase of Intelsat, combining roughly 90 GEO satellites, 30 MEO satellites, and LEO access into a single multi-orbit operator. Amazon announced in April 2026 that it would acquire Globalstar for approximately $11.57 billion, securing globally licensed MSS spectrum and a 24-satellite constellation to underpin its Leo broadband and direct-to-device push. And now Rocket Lab has bought Iridium for $8 billion.

The common denominator is spectrum. Industry analysts have been explicit: mobile satellite services spectrum is no longer a niche technical asset, it is high-value orbital real estate. The holdings of Globalstar, Iridium, and Viasat are particularly valuable because they benefit from decades of quasi-global regulatory coordination that new entrants cannot replicate quickly. When trillion-dollar companies, Amazon, SpaceX, are willing to write nine- and ten-figure cheques for spectrum licences attached to aging satellite fleets, they are telling you what they believe the bottleneck is. It is not launch. It is not hardware. It is the legal right to transmit.

Rocket Lab's management clearly read the same signal. Peter Beck told Bloomberg the deal was about acquiring assets "that would take years and billions of dollars to build independently." That is not hyperbole, it is a factual description of what globally licensed L-band spectrum with pole-to-pole coverage takes to assemble. In a sector where the three largest players are consolidating spectrum and networks at speed, standing still was the riskiest option available.

WHAT IRIDIUM ACTUALLY IS — AND WHY IT IS HARD TO REPLICATE

Most equity investors in the space sector have never looked closely at Iridium. Here is what Rocket Lab is buying.

Iridium operates a constellation of 66 active low-Earth-orbit satellites and 14 on-orbit spares, 80 spacecraft at approximately 780 km altitude, providing truly global coverage including both poles. It is the only commercial satellite network on Earth with complete pole-to-pole reach. The constellation uses inter-satellite crosslinks, meaning traffic can be routed between satellites in space before being sent to a ground station. For the US military, this is critical: all EMSS (Enhanced Mobile Satellite Services) traffic is routed to a dedicated, US-government-owned and operated gateway, meaning mission-critical communications never touch foreign soil.

Iridium ended 2025 with approximately 2.5 million billable subscribers. Its customer base is not consumer broadband, it is the military, government agencies, airlines, shipping companies, mining operations, and industrial IoT networks that operate where terrestrial coverage does not exist. These are customers for whom satellite connectivity is not a nice-to-have but a contractual or regulatory requirement. Aireon, which Iridium acquired outright in May 2026 for $367 million, provides space-based ADS-B aircraft tracking to air-navigation service providers globally, a safety-of-life service that is now mandated for oceanic surveillance.

In 2024, Iridium acquired Satelles, adding authenticated positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) services that function as a backup to GPS, relevant at a moment when GPS jamming and spoofing are increasingly common in military and commercial contexts. Iridium announced a compact PNT ASIC chip in late 2025 designed for integration into consumer, industrial, and government devices.

The spectrum itself, L-band, globally licensed, is the asset that would be most expensive and time-consuming to replicate. L-band operates at lower frequencies than Starlink's Ka/Ku-band, which means lower throughput but significantly better signal propagation through foliage, walls, weather, and building interiors. This is why L-band anchors tactical military communications, aviation safety systems, maritime distress, and IoT rather than consumer broadband. Craig-Hallum was the most specific analyst on this point: Iridium's spectrum is "designed for low-bandwidth, high-reliability use cases like tactical communications and IoT, not broadband internet." The Starlink comparison is the "wrong take."

THE FINANCIAL PROFILE: WHAT THE NUMBERS ACTUALLY SAY

Iridium is profitable. This alone sets it apart from most of the space stocks.

In 2025, Iridium reported total revenue of approximately $872 million and net income of $114 million. Full-year Operational EBITDA was $495.3 million, up 5% year-over-year. Service revenue, the recurring, subscription-based component, was approximately 75% of total revenue. Pro forma free cash flow was $296 million in 2025, with management guiding to approximately $318 million in 2026 at a 66% EBITDA-to-cash conversion rate, and a cumulative $1.5–$1.8 billion free cash flow target through the end of the decade. Net leverage closed 2025 at 3.4x OEBITDA, trending toward 3.0x by year-end 2026 and below 2.0x by decade-end. For 2026, guidance is flat-to-2% service revenue growth and OEBITDA of $480–$490 million (the modest step-down reflecting a shift to all-cash compensation rather than an operational decline).

Compare that to what Rocket Lab looked like before the deal. Q1 2026 revenue was a record $200.3 million, up 63% year-over-year, with backlog exceeding $2.2 billion. But EBITDA was negative. Free cash flow was negative. Revenue was project-based, every dollar had to be won through competitive launch contracts and spacecraft orders. The market rewarded the growth trajectory with a roughly $60 billion market cap, pricing RKLB at approximately 60x forward sales. That multiple was built on narrative and trajectory, not profit.

The deal transforms the financial character of the combined entity overnight. Rocket Lab goes from zero EBITDA to approximately $500 million. From zero free cash flow to roughly $300 million. From zero recurring revenue to a subscription base generating approximately $630 million of service revenue a year from 2.5 million paying subscribers. The growth story does not go away, Electron, Neutron, space systems, and the $2.2 billion backlog are all still there. But they are now layered on top of a profitable, cash-generative utility rather than standing alone as the entire investment case.

THE GOVERNMENT MOAT

The part of the deal that is hardest to value, and arguably the most strategically significant, is Iridium's relationship with the US Department of Defence. The EMSS programme is not a single contract; it is a suite of three core agreements with the US Space Force that collectively provide unlimited voice and narrowband data for an unlimited number of DoD and federal government users. The EMSS Airtime Contract operates as a "family plan" for military SATCOM, no usage caps, no subscriber limits, all traffic routed through a secure US government-owned gateway. Alongside it, the ECS3 sustainment contract (approximately $94–$103 million over five years, awarded April 2024) ensures the ground infrastructure stays operational, and the SITH infrastructure transformation contract (up to $85.8 million over five years, awarded December 2025) funds technology refreshes and security upgrades.

These are not the kind of contracts that switch providers easily. The DoD has been an Iridium customer since the original constellation, through the company's bankruptcy and restructuring, through the NEXT upgrade campaign, and into the current programme. Iridium is described internally as a "line item on the annual DoD budget." For a company like Rocket Lab that is already a NASA VADR awardee and US Space Force NSSL Phase 3 participant, inheriting Iridium's defence relationships adds an entirely different category of government revenue, recurring, high-trust, and deeply embedded in the US military's communications architecture.

There is also a national-security logic that goes beyond Iridium's own contracts. In a world where the US government is increasingly dependent on commercial space infrastructure, the concentration risk of relying on a single provider, SpaceX, is a policy concern, not just a market concern. A vertically integrated Rocket Lab that can design, build, launch, and operate its own constellation provides the alternative that defence planners need. This is the strategic context that makes the deal about more than revenue arithmetic.

WHAT IT COSTS — AND WHETHER THE PRICE MAKES SENSE

The $54 per share offer, $27.00 cash plus Rocket Lab stock via an exchange ratio collared at $67.50–$112.50, represents a 24% premium to Iridium's 26 June close and implies an enterprise value of approximately $8 billion. On 2025 OEBITDA of $495 million, that is roughly 16x EBITDA. On 2025 pro forma free cash flow of $296 million, it is approximately 27x FCF.

Is that expensive? Context matters. Amazon paid approximately $11.57 billion for Globalstar, a company with significantly lower revenue (~$273 million in 2025) and a less mature network. SpaceX paid approximately $17 billion for EchoStar's spectrum alone, without the operating business. At 16x EBITDA for a profitable, globally licensed, defence-embedded satellite operator with $300 million of annual free cash flow, Rocket Lab's price is within precedent, and arguably cheaper per dollar of cash flow than either comparable transaction.

The stock component is significant but strategically rational. At RKLB's current price of approximately $100, the deal implies issuing a substantial number of new shares. But Rocket Lab is using equity that the market prices at 60x forward sales to buy a business at 16x EBITDA, textbook financial engineering. If the combined entity earns a blended multiple even modestly higher than what Iridium would command standalone, the deal is accretive to shareholders despite the dilution. Every analyst who published a reaction made exactly this observation.

WHAT COULD GO WRONG

Integration risk is the primary concern. Rocket Lab has never absorbed a business this large. Iridium has approximately 900 employees, a McLean, Virginia headquarters, established government contracting relationships, and a culture built around network operations rather than hardware manufacturing. Merging these organisations while maintaining service quality for 2.5 million subscribers and sensitive DoD customers is non-trivial. History is full of strategically brilliant acquisitions that were operationally botched.

Neutron dependency. Part of the long-term synergy case is launching future Iridium constellation replacements on Neutron rather than buying rides from competitors. Neutron has not yet flown. If its development timeline slips, the cost synergies that justify the premium are delayed. That said, Iridium's current constellation was completed in 2019 and is designed for a multi-decade operational life; a next-generation replacement is years away, giving Neutron time to mature.

Leverage. The $27 per share cash component implies a significant debt raise. Iridium itself already carries net leverage of 3.4x OEBITDA. The combined entity's leverage will need to be managed carefully, particularly if Rocket Lab's core launch and space systems business remains free-cash-flow negative during the integration period. The counterbalance is Iridium's own deleveraging trajectory: the business was on track to reach below 2.0x by decade-end on a standalone basis.

Regulatory and timeline risk. The deal requires Iridium shareholder approval and regulatory clearance, with closing expected mid-2027. Iridium's spectrum licences, government contracts, and the involvement of foreign satellite ground stations introduce regulatory complexity. The deal falling through, while unlikely given board unanimity and the 24% premium, would leave Rocket Lab having expended significant management attention and deal costs.

WHAT IT MEANS FOR THE REST OF THE BASKET

This is where the deal becomes relevant to every name your portfolio touches, not just RKLB.

The consolidation wave has now claimed four of the sector's major satellite operators in under a year. The remaining independent players, Viasat, Telesat, and the handful of smaller MSS operators, are now operating in a market where their three largest competitors (SpaceX, Amazon, Rocket Lab post-close) are vertically integrated and backed by either a trillion-dollar balance sheet or an extremely high-multiple equity currency. The strategic pressure to find a partner, a buyer, or a differentiated niche has never been higher.

For ASTS, the implications are competitive. Iridium's L-band is not direct-to-device broadband, Craig-Hallum is right about that, but the deal does give Rocket Lab a platform from which to expand into D2D and IoT over time, using Iridium's globally licensed spectrum as the foundation. AST's advantage remains its broadband-class, unmodified-smartphone approach, but the runway is getting more crowded.

For MDA, the deal is potentially positive. MDA builds satellites, including for Globalstar's next-generation constellation. A vertically integrated Rocket Lab that needs to eventually replace Iridium's constellation could either build those satellites in-house (using its own space systems division) or contract them out. MDA's relationship with the broader ecosystem means it could be a partner or a competitor on the hardware side.

For the defence-adjacent names (LUNR, FLY, RDW), the signal is strategic: the companies that are consolidating into full-stack platforms are the ones the market is rewarding. The names that remain single-capability pure plays, launch only, components only, imagery only, face a structural question about whether they can sustain premium multiples in a sector where the winners do everything.

Takeaway: The Iridium deal is not "Rocket Lab vs Starlink." L-band and Ka-band serve different markets, and anyone framing the acquisition as a broadband play has misread the asset. What the deal actually is, is Rocket Lab's entry into the same structural category as SpaceX: a company that designs, builds, launches, and operates its own satellites on its own network, generating recurring revenue from a global subscriber base with deep government relationships. The price, $8 billion, roughly 16x EBITDA, is defensible in the context of a consolidation wave where Amazon paid more for less cash flow and SpaceX paid more for spectrum alone. The risk is execution: integration, Neutron, leverage. The opportunity is transformation: from a high-growth, zero-profit launch company into a vertically integrated space utility with approximately $500 million of EBITDA and $300 million of free cash flow, anchored by the US military's most trusted satellite communications network.
